headline: Payrolls land on a market still bleeding from Thursday's AI rout: Nasdaq-100 futures are bouncing ≈+1.7% after a 5.5% drop and a 12% SOX collapse, but Asia followed through (Nikkei ≈−6%, Kospi −6–8%). The 2Y is pinned at 4.47% with December hike odds ≈66–69%, down from 82%, so a print near the 59–65k consensus decides whether the front end re-steepens hike pricing or keeps unwinding it.
summary: The damage report: Thursday the S&P 500 fell 4.36% to 7,353.73, the Dow 1,833 points to 51,523.06 and the Nasdaq Comp. 5.52% to 24,315.00, a correction and (per WSJ) the largest one-day dollar loss in Nasdaq history at ≈$2.5T. The SOX closed ≈−12.2% at ≈9,011, XLK −8.0% (worst since Mar 2020) and the Russell 2000 −4.45% to 2,729.89. The trigger is the Democratic sweep: investors are pricing slower data-center buildout under a hostile Congress and local zoning revolts.

Overnight was mixed: Asia followed Thursday down (Nikkei ≈−6% into a bear market, Kospi −6% to −8% with a trading halt, TSMC ≈−9.6%), and the Stoxx 600 is ≈−1%. US futures split. CNBC has Nasdaq-100 ≈+1.7% and S&P ≈+0.4%, but Dow ≈−0.9% as Wednesday's value/'blue-wave' rotation partly reverses. Airbnb (≈+7–12%) and Cloudflare (≈+17%) are up after hours, while DraftKings, Five9 (≈−18%), Atlassian (≈−16%) and Axon (≈−14%) are down.

Rates are holding Thursday's bull steepener (short yields falling faster than long ones). The 2Y is 4.474% (flat), the 10Y 4.83% and the 30Y 5.249%, so 2s10s is ≈+36 bp. Swaps and FedWatch price ≈66–69% for a Dec 8–9 hike vs ≈82% on Wednesday. Logan (Oct 30: 'at least two more' 25 bp hikes) and Musalem (8:10 AM CT today) are the hawkish anchors. Bowman speaks on supervision at 11:15 AM CT.

7:30 AM CT payrolls: consensus is 59k (Dow Jones) / 65k (Bloomberg) vs 29k prior, with unemployment 4.2% and AHE ≈+0.3% m/m. Whisper numbers run to ≈82k. A beat with 0.3% wages likely pushes December back toward 80%. A sub-30k print would make the market doubt the hike cycle entirely, steepen 2s10s further and support gold. UMich prelim (≈47–48 vs 48.0) follows at 9:00 AM, with inflation expectations the key line.

Cross-asset: Brent settled Thursday at $98.29 (+$3.67) and touched ≈$99.95 overnight on Middle East tanker attacks (still ≈−15% on the week), with WTI ≈$90.7. Gold is ≈$4,072 (−0.4%) after a ≈$250 week. LME copper is $13,738/t (−0.8%), headed for its worst week since March (−2.9%) on the data-center selloff, even as SHFE stocks fell 24% to a near-3-year low. DXY is ≈101.6–101.9.

Capital markets: the AI backlash is hitting the IPO calendar. Reuters says Anthropic's roadshow, planned for next week, is in doubt, and WSJ reports anchor investors pushing the $1.5T target toward ≈$1T. IG credit is still open: Apple priced $7.5B in seven tranches on ≈$31B of orders. Banks face years of oversight, with Warren expected to chair Senate Banking from January. JPM fell 4.1% Thursday.
markets_asof: Pre-market ≈6:20 AM CT (futures/yields/commodities); index levels are Thu close

markets.label: PHLX Semis (SOX)
markets.note: Thu close; worst day since Apr 2025

calendar.why: He is the FOMC's center of gravity. No coverage of his remarks was found before publication, so check headlines for any December signal.

This is the last payrolls before the Dec 8–9 FOMC. With hike odds already cut from 82% to ≈66–69%, the front end is asymmetric: a beat re-prices hikes fast, and a miss makes the market doubt the cycle.
Wages matter as much as the headline. 0.3% m/m with ISM services prices at 73 keeps the inflation case for hiking alive.
This is the first hawk on air after payrolls. Listen for whether he dismisses the equity rout as a financial-conditions issue.
Watch the 1Y/5–10Y inflation expectations with Brent near $100 again, since unanchored expectations are the Fed hawks' strongest argument.

calendar.event: Fed: Bowman (Vice Chair for Supervision), Univ. of Mississippi
calendar.why: She is speaking on supervision and regulation the week Democrats won Congress. It's a read on capital rules (Basel re-proposal, SLR) and how banks will be regulated.
It's a second-tier read on household leverage, which matters for card and consumer-lending banks.
After Thursday the market is punishing guidance cuts hard: DraftKings and Axon fell 14–18% after hours.
Today's payrolls and the Nov CPI decide it.
This tests whether the haven bid into the long end survives supply, with the 30Y at ≈5.25%.

rates.title: Curve holds bull steepener into payrolls
rates.body: The 2Y is 4.474%, 10Y 4.83% and 30Y 5.249%, all within ≈1 bp of Thursday's close after the 2Y dropped ≈11 bp in the rout. A BMO client survey shows 48% ready to buy dips in Treasuries vs a 43% six-month average.
rates.simple: A bull steepener means short-term yields (the interest on bonds) fell faster than long-term ones, which happens when traders think the Fed will hike less. Investors fled stocks into two-year notes because those are most sensitive to Fed decisions. That lowers the rates banks and borrowers pay on short-term loans.

rates.title: December hike odds cut to ≈2-in-3
rates.body: FedWatch/swaps price ≈66–69% for a 25 bp hike on Dec 8–9 vs ≈82% Wednesday, with fed funds at 3.75–4.00%. Logan said Oct 30 she wants 'at least two more' 25 bp hikes and then a pause, and Musalem has argued for more tightening.
rates.simple: FedWatch reads the chance of a rate change from futures prices (contracts that bet on future rates). Before the crash, the market was nearly sure of a December hike. A stock-market shock makes the Fed less likely to tighten. Officials keep saying inflation is the bigger risk, so today's jobs data is the tiebreaker.

rates.title: Global long ends rally with the US
rates.body: Gilt 10Y yields hit ≈5.10%, the lowest since August, a day after the BoE hiked to 4.00%. JGB 10Y yields eased to ≈2.6–2.8%, the lowest since July, as the Nikkei fell ≈6%, and Bunds were ≈3.22–3.26%.
rates.simple: When stocks crash worldwide, investors buy government bonds everywhere, pushing their yields down. Britain's central bank just raised rates, yet its long bonds still rallied, which shows fear of a slowdown beating fear of inflation for now. Lower global yields make U.S. Treasuries look relatively attractive to foreign buyers.

derivatives.title: CME prints record October: 30M contracts/day
derivatives.body: October ADV hit 30.0M contracts (+15% y/y), beating the 26.3M record from Oct 2025. Interest-rate ADV was 14.8M, equity index 8.8M and energy 2.7M, and 30Y bond futures rose 52% to 625k/day.
derivatives.simple: ADV (average daily volume) counts how many futures and options contracts change hands per day. Rate contracts are half the total because companies and funds are hedging an uncertain Fed path. Record activity means more fees for CME and shows how much risk the market is moving around.

derivatives.title: Asset managers hold record Treasury-futures longs; vol elevated
derivatives.body: CME's November Rates Recap shows asset managers added ≈630k contracts of net-long Treasury futures from Sep 22 to Oct 27, reaching a record ≈3M net long in 10Y notes. CME's Treasury vol gauge rose from 87 (Sep 4) to a 7-month high of 140 on Oct 22, and cleared USD swaps were +76% y/y.
derivatives.simple: Being 'net long' means funds own more bond futures than they've sold, so they profit if yields fall. They are the mirror image of hedge funds running the basis trade (buying cash bonds, selling futures). Crowded positions plus high volatility (how much prices swing) can amplify moves around a surprise jobs number.

derivatives.title: VIX shock and forced deleveraging
derivatives.body: The VIX had its largest point jump since Apr 4, 2025 (+11.57) and closed ≈28, while XLK fell 8.04%. Goldman's Timothy Moe blamed Asia's follow-through on forced unwinds and stop-loss selling (automatic sell orders), with the Kospi down 6–8% and halted.
derivatives.simple: The VIX is the 'fear gauge,' built from what investors pay for S&P 500 options (insurance against big moves). When it spikes, dealers who sold that insurance must hedge by selling stocks, which can feed the drop. That is why a strong-but-not-hot jobs number could calm markets quickly.

metals.title: Gold consolidates below $4,100 after a $250 week
metals.body: Spot gold was ≈$4,071.50 (−0.38%) at 4:41 AM ET after topping $4,146.9 Thursday. It's still ≈+5.9% on the week on a weaker dollar after the election, falling yields and fading hike odds.
metals.simple: Gold pays no interest, so it does best when real yields (bond interest minus inflation) fall and the dollar weakens. Both happened this week. A hot jobs number would raise yields and pressure gold, and a weak one would likely push it back above $4,100.

metals.title: Copper heads for worst week since March on AI fears
metals.body: LME 3M copper is $13,738/t (−0.8%), −2.9% on the week, with a low of $13,663. Physical China is tight: SHFE stocks fell 24% this week to 33,848t and the Yangshan premium matched its $210/t record. COMEX inventories sit at a record ≈731k t.
metals.simple: Copper wires every data center, so traders sold it along with chip stocks on fears the AI buildout slows. But Chinese warehouses are emptying and buyers there are paying record premiums for physical metal, which says real demand is solid. A Democratic Congress also lowers the odds of a U.S. copper tariff, which would erode the COMEX premium.

metals.title: Central banks and ETFs keep the floor under gold
metals.body: WGC data has the PBOC adding 23t in September, its biggest month since Oct 2023, for a 23-month streak and 2,410t (8.5% of reserves); Kitco reports a different figure. Global gold ETFs added 19t in October to 4,275t, while North America was the only region with outflows (−$512M).
metals.simple: Central banks like China's buy gold to diversify away from dollars, and they buy steadily regardless of price. ETFs (funds that trade like stocks and hold physical gold) show what investors are doing. U.S. investors trimmed, but Asia and Europe bought.

metals.title: Silver lags gold as the industrial side cracks
metals.body: Silver slipped ≈0.8% to ≈$51.65 late Thursday while gold held gains. Platinum (≈$1,520–1,525) and palladium (≈$1,030) quotes from Kitco and MetalCharts conflict on direction.
metals.simple: Silver is half precious metal and half industrial input (solar panels, electronics), so it trades partly like copper. On a day when tech and data-center stocks crashed, its industrial side pulled it down even as gold's safe-haven role held up. The gold/silver ratio widening is a classic risk-off signal.

banking.title: Anthropic IPO timing and price in doubt
banking.body: Reuters reports prospective investors doubt next week's planned roadshow will go ahead after the AI selloff. WSJ says anchors want the $1.5T valuation cut toward ≈$1T and the up-to-$100B raise possibly trimmed to ≈$80B, and Kalshi filing-by-Nov-30 odds fell from 84% to 60%.
banking.simple: An IPO roadshow is when bankers pitch a company to big investors before it lists. This would be the largest IPO ever, so the fees (often 1–2% of the raise for mega-deals, lower here) are huge for the underwriting banks. If tech stocks keep falling, buyers demand a lower price or the deal waits, and that's ECM (equity capital markets) desks' biggest risk this quarter.

banking.title: Apple taps IG market for $7.5B through the rout
banking.body: Apple sold a seven-part, $7.5B investment-grade bond on ≈$31B of orders (≈4x covered) on the day the S&P fell 4.4%. In Europe, IG yields are +30 bp since September to ≈4.4% and high yield +90 bp to ≈7%.
banking.simple: Investment-grade means bonds from the safest companies. Even on a crash day, investors lined up to lend to Apple, so debt markets are open for top names. Riskier companies' borrowing costs are climbing, which slows leveraged buyouts and the bank fees that come with them.

banking.title: Democratic sweep ends banks' deregulatory run
banking.body: Warren is expected to chair Senate Banking from January 2027 and has asked regulators to withdraw three capital proposals. TD Securities says the favorable-legislation window has likely closed, and TD Cowen doesn't see the CLARITY crypto bill passing within two years. JPM fell 4.1% to ≈$337.75 Thursday, erasing its post-election gain.
banking.simple: Banks hoped for looser capital rules (how much of their own money they must hold against losses). Congress now flips to a party that wants tougher oversight, though the regulators themselves stay the same until their terms run out. Tighter capital means less room for buybacks and lending growth.

banking.title: Community bank M&A keeps grinding: Illinois buyer among three deals
banking.body: Mattoon, IL-based First Mid Bancshares will buy Evergreen Bancshares (MO; $932M assets) for $70.7M in cash and stock. First Community Bankshares will pay $243M in stock for Main Street Financial (OH). YTD, 162 bank acquisitions were announced through Nov 2.
banking.simple: Small banks merge to spread compliance and technology costs over more deposits. Paying partly in stock means the seller's owners share the risk if the combined bank underperforms. Steady deal flow keeps FIG (financial institutions group) bankers busy even when big-bank M&A is quiet.

banking.title: Strategic M&A still printing: Shield–Echodyne $5.3B
banking.body: Shield AI agreed to buy radar maker Echodyne for $4.8B at close plus up to $500M in earnouts, closing early 2027. Adani Ports is buying Evos for a ≈€2.56B EV with MUFG as sole underwriter on up to €2.8B of debt.
banking.simple: An earnout is extra money paid later only if the acquired company hits targets, which bridges price disagreements. Defense tech is a sector where buyers keep paying up regardless of the AI selloff. One bank underwriting the whole financing shows lenders still compete hard to win big deals.

cnbc.title: $1T+ wiped from megacaps in AI rout
cnbc.body: The Magnificent 7 lost >$1T in value Thursday, with Nvidia −9% (≈$440B) and Tesla −10.8%. XLK fell 8.04%, its worst day since Mar 16, 2020, and NYSE decliners beat advancers 2,344 to 416.
cnbc.simple: A handful of giant tech companies make up a big share of the S&P 500, so when they fall together, the whole index drops. Nearly every stock fell, not just tech, which shows broad panic rather than a single-company problem. That hits retirement accounts and the wealth effect behind consumer spending.

cnbc.title: Futures claw back before jobs data
cnbc.body: Nasdaq-100 futures were ≈+1.7% and S&P ≈+0.4% early, with Dow ≈−0.9%, as Nvidia, Amazon, Tesla and Alphabet bounced premarket. The Nasdaq is officially in correction (>10% off its Oct 6 high).
cnbc.simple: Futures trade before the stock market opens and hint at where it will start. A 'correction' is a 10% drop from a peak. Bounces after big drops are common, but the jobs report at 7:30 AM CT can erase or extend them.

cnbc.title: Asia's chip giants crushed
cnbc.body: The Kospi fell 6–8% with a trading halt, the Nikkei ≈6% into a bear market and TSMC ≈9.6%, after the SOX's 12.2% drop. Goldman's Moe blamed forced unwinds and stop-loss selling.
cnbc.simple: Korea, Japan and Taiwan's markets are built around chip makers that supply U.S. AI companies, so a U.S. AI scare hits them hardest. A bear market is a 20% fall from the peak. Forced selling by leveraged traders can push prices below what fundamentals justify.

cnbc.title: Why the election hit AI: a 'war of attrition' on data centers
cnbc.body: CNBC's read is that a Democratic Congress plus local wins against data-center projects threaten the AI buildout's pace. That puts chipmakers, hyperscalers and power/infrastructure names at risk.
cnbc.simple: Data centers need huge amounts of land, power and water, and many voters opposed them. If permits and power hookups slow, AI companies spend less on chips. That's why a political result hit tech stocks this hard.

wsj.title: Anthropic IPO investors balk at $1.5T
wsj.body: Three large prospective buyers told WSJ they expect the valuation to come down, possibly toward ≈$1T. A delay or a smaller raise (≈$80B floated) is possible.
wsj.simple: When stock prices of similar companies fall, investors won't pay as much for a new one. A $500B valuation cut would be one of the largest repricings ever on a single deal. It also shows how much AI enthusiasm has cooled in 48 hours.

wsj.title: Nasdaq's biggest one-day value loss ever
wsj.body: WSJ put Thursday's loss at ≈$2.5T of Nasdaq market value, the largest single-day dollar drop in its history, on a 5.52% decline.
wsj.simple: Measured in dollars, it's a record because the companies are so much bigger now. In percentage terms it was the worst day since April 2025, not the worst ever. It's still a big hit to investor wealth.

wsj.title: Editorial: voters turned on data centers
wsj.body: The WSJ editorial board tied the rout to campaign hostility toward data centers and to Democratic control of Congress and many statehouses. It named chipmakers, cloud firms and builders as the biggest losers.
wsj.simple: The paper argues the selloff is a policy story, not just a valuation one. If states make data centers harder to build, the companies that sell to them lose expected future sales. That's a lasting risk, not a one-day mood swing.

wsj.title: CVS to split off its drugstores
wsj.body: CVS will separate ≈9,000 retail stores, MinuteClinic and mail order from Aetna/Caremark/Specialty by 1H 2028. Shares fell ≈12.5–13% on Nov 4.
wsj.simple: A spin-off creates two separately traded companies so each can be valued on its own. Investors sold because the retail business is shrinking and the split costs money. It means years of advisory and financing work for banks.

tribune.title: CME Group logs record October volume
tribune.body: Chicago-based CME averaged 30.0M contracts a day in October (+15% y/y). Rates were 14.8M, 30Y bond futures +52% to 625k and crypto 145k/day (≈$7.85B notional).
tribune.simple: CME runs the exchanges where futures on rates, stocks, oil and grain trade. When the economy and Fed are uncertain, more people hedge, so CME earns more fees. Its volume is a good gauge of how nervous markets are.

tribune.title: ADM beats and raises on biofuels
tribune.body: ADM posted Q3 adjusted EPS of $1.77 vs $0.92 a year ago on $22.34B revenue. Ag Services & Oilseeds profit rose 105% to $778M, and FY guidance went to $5.50–5.80 from $5.15–5.60.
tribune.simple: ADM processes crops like soybeans into food and fuel. Government biofuel rules raised demand for soybean oil, which widened the margin (crush spread) between what ADM pays for beans and what it sells products for. Higher guidance means management expects that to last.

tribune.title: $20B Joliet data center in jeopardy over ComEd power guarantee
tribune.body: The developer offered ComEd $1 toward a $587M power-infrastructure guarantee, putting the project at risk. It's a local example of the power-cost fight behind this week's AI selloff.
tribune.simple: Utilities spend heavily on new lines and substations for data centers and want guarantees they'll be paid back if the project fails. Otherwise ordinary customers could get stuck with the bill. Fights like this are why investors worry data-center growth will slow.

tribune.title: Medline cuts 304 jobs, exits hospital beds
tribune.body: Northfield-based Medline will lay off 304 people starting Nov 17 and wind down its home-care bed business after a recall.
tribune.simple: A recall forces a company to pull a faulty product. Medline decided fixing the business wasn't worth it. It's a reminder that recalls hit jobs and earnings, not just reputation.

nyt.title: Voters rejected AI; scrutiny era begins
nyt.body: Democrats campaigned on regulating AI, and voters turned down data-center projects. Ohio alone had 21 data-center ballot questions across 18 communities.
nyt.simple: Local referendums let residents block zoning for big projects. Combined with a Congress open to regulating AI, tech firms face slower and costlier expansion. That's the political root of Thursday's market drop.

nyt.title: Toyota soars on hybrids and a weak yen
nyt.body: Toyota posted its first profit gain in six quarters and raised its outlook ≈15%. Shares jumped ≈14–16%, the biggest gain in nearly 40 years. NYT notes US hybrid sales rose 28% in Q3 while EV sales fell 40%.
nyt.simple: A weak yen makes Japanese exports cheaper abroad and their dollar profits worth more at home. High gas prices pushed buyers to hybrids, where Toyota leads. It was one of the few big winners on a day Japan's market crashed.

nyt.title: AI fears erase the post-election rally
nyt.body: NYT framed Thursday as AI worries wiping out Wednesday's rally, with the S&P's worst day in more than a year (−4.36%).
nyt.simple: Wednesday investors cheered the election for banks and small companies. Thursday they focused on what it means for AI spending. Markets can swing fast when a new government's impact is still being figured out.

nyt.title: NYT Co. in talks to buy Letterboxd for ≈$330M
nyt.body: The Times is in exclusive talks to buy Letterboxd for ≈$330M, ≈20x projected 2026 earnings of ≈$15M, from controlling holder Tiny. No deal is signed.
nyt.simple: Paying 20 times earnings means the buyer expects strong growth. The Times is building a bundle of subscription products (games, cooking, sports) and wants a younger audience. It's a small deal but a template for media M&A.

talking_points.point: With December hike odds already cut from ≈82% to ≈66–69% on an equity shock rather than data, the 2Y at 4.47% has more room to sell off on a beat than to rally on a miss. That's the case for fading the move in SOFR Dec/Mar futures if NFP prints ≥65k with 0.3% AHE. I'd watch whether the curve bear-flattens (front-end yields rising faster) and erases Thursday's ≈11 bp 2Y rally.

LME copper is having its worst week since March (−2.9% to ≈$13,738/t) on data-center fears, yet SHFE stocks fell 24% to a near-3-year low and the Yangshan premium is at a record $210/t. Meanwhile COMEX stocks are a record ≈731k t, and a Democratic Congress lowers 232-tariff odds. That's an argument for the COMEX–LME spread compressing.

The market sold JPM 4.1% in one day, but the bigger question for 2027 is capital: Warren chairing Senate Banking pressures the Basel re-proposal and SLR relief, while regulators stay in place. Meanwhile the deal calendar is bifurcated: Apple's $7.5B IG deal was ≈4x covered even as Anthropic's ≈$1–1.5T IPO wobbles. Rates and credit desks keep earning in volatility (CME record 30M ADV) while ECM fees are the exposed line.

caveats: WSJ, NYT and the Tribune are paywalled or unreachable, and this session could not open CNBC, Kitco, Yahoo or FXStreet pages directly, so figures come from search-result summaries and syndicated or secondary coverage (outlets named per story). Futures percentages conflict across sources (Dow −0.6% to −0.9%; Nasdaq-100 +0.8% to +1.8%). The VIX's Thursday % gain is reported as both ≈+39% and ≈+70%. Thursday's brief listed Brent ≈$96 and silver ≈$52.85; settles were Brent $98.29 and silver ≈$51.65 late. PBOC September gold buying differs between WGC (23t) and Kitco (21t). KBW bank index and COMEX copper levels were not found. Williams' and Logan's latest remarks were not found. Tribune-bucket stories come from Crain's, CME and SEC filings, and some are 2–9 days old.
